content.content: 1 # Keynote Pro manual (the engine behind present-in-html) 2 3 Paths below are the engine's. In this skill: `check.mjs` and `tools/*.mjs` are in `scripts/`; `template.html`, 4 `library/` and `examples/` are in `assets/`. Build tools and the sample decks mentioned here are not shipped with the skill. 5 6 - 1. Write a deck in 60 seconds 7 - 2. Layout cheat-sheet (shortest working snippet for each) 8 - 3. Deck recipes (theme, fonts, sequence, builds) 9 - 4. Theme design plans (DESIGN.md format) 10 - 5. Builds, transitions, Magic Move 11 - 6. Diagrams that draw 12 - 6b. Images 13 - 7. Presenter keys and tools 14 - 8. PDF and print 15 - 9. Right-to-left and Arabic 16 - 10. Checker 17 - 12. Checklist before you present 18 - 12a. Narration (recorded voice per slide) 19 - 12b. Slides that run 20 - 13. Known limits 21 22 ## 1. Write a deck in 60 seconds 23 24 1. Copy `template.html`. Set `data-theme` (and optionally `data-fonts`) on ``, and the title in `` and `data-title` on `<main class="deck">`. 25 2. Delete the sample slides. Add `<section class="slide" data-layout="...">` blocks (cheat-sheet below). 26 3. Add `<aside class="notes"><p>...</p></aside>` inside any slide for presenter notes. 27 4. `node check.mjs my-deck.html`, fix what it lists, open it, press **P**. 28 29 Rules of thumb: one idea per slide; at most 5 bullets; say the number, not the paragraph. Layouts auto-fit 30 (type shrinks to 78% before content would leave the safe area, and short content grows, up to 1.25x on bullets and 1.5x on statements, so a slide is never half empty), lists balance their wrapping, images crop with 31 `object-fit: cover`. You never tune CSS to make text fit; if `check.mjs` still complains, cut words. 32 33 ## 2. Layout cheat-sheet (shortest working snippet for each) 34 35 Every snippet goes inside `<section class="slide" data-layout="NAME"> ... </section>`. Optional extras are in comments. 36 37 ```html 38 <!-- title --> <h1>Title with <em>one accent</em></h1><p class="sub">Subtitle</p> 39 <!-- <p class="label">Event</p> <p class="meta"><span>Name</span><span>Date</span></p> --> 40 <!-- section --> <h2>Part two</h2> <!-- <p class="label">Part two</p> <span class="num">2</span> <p>One-line promise</p> --> 41 <!-- statement --> <h2>One huge sentence with an <em>accent</em>.</h2> 42 <!-- agenda --> <h2>Agenda</h2><ol><li>Results <small>10 min</small></li><li>Plan</li></ol> <!-- aria-current on an li dims the rest --> 43 <!-- bullets --> <h2>Title</h2><ul data-build="list"><li><strong>Lead.</strong> Support.</li><li>Two</li><li>Three</li></ul> 44 <!-- two-column --> <h2>Title</h2><div class="col"><h3>A</h3><p>Text</p></div><div class="col"><h3>B</h3><ul><li>x</li></ul></div> 45 <!-- image-left --> <figure><img src="a.jpg" alt=""></figure><h2>Title</h2><p>Text</p> <!-- empty <figure></figure> = placeholder art --> 46 <!-- image-right --> (same markup, mirrored) 47 <!-- full-bleed --> <h2>Title on a photo</h2> <!-- data-bg="photo.jpg" on the section, or <img class="bleed" src alt=""> --> 48 <!-- big-number --> <div class="big" data-build="count">98<small>%</small></div><p>One honest caption.</p> <!-- <p class="src">Source</p> --> 49 <!-- stats --> <h2>Title</h2><div class="stat"><b>4.2M</b><span>Users</span></div> ...2 to 4 of these 50 <!-- chart --> <h2>Title</h2><p class="lede">Takeaway</p> 51 <figure class="chart" data-chart="column" data-values="Q1:12,Q2:18,Q3:21"></figure> 52 <!-- data-chart: column | bar | line. Multi-series: put a <table> inside (header row + label column). 53 data-prefix="$" data-unit="M" data-decimals="1" data-highlight="3" (1-based or a label) 54 data-min="92" (line charts only) data-build="draw" (bars grow, lines draw) 55 data-wide on the section = full-width plot; <figcaption>Source</figcaption> --> 56 <!-- comparison --> <h2>Title</h2><table><thead><tr><th></th><th>A</th><th class="rec" data-tag="Recommended">B</th></tr></thead> 57 <tbody><tr><th>Price</th><td>$1</td><td>$2</td></tr></tbody></table> 58 <!-- timeline --> <h2>Title</h2><ol class="timeline" data-build="list"><li><time>Q1</time><h3>Step</h3><p>Detail</p></li>...</ol> <!-- class="now" marks today --> 59 <!-- process --> <h2>Title</h2><ol class="steps" data-build="list"><li><h3>Capture</h3><p>Detail</p></li>...</ol> <!-- 3 to 5 steps --> 60 <!-- quote --> <blockquote>The quote with an <em>accent</em>.</blockquote><cite><b>Name</b>Title, Company</cite> 61 <!-- code --> <h2>Title</h2><pre data-lang="js" data-focus="1-2;4-6;*"> code </pre> <!-- indent freely; focus steps light lines per click --> 62 <!-- team --> <h2>Team</h2><div class="people"><figure class="person" data-initials="AK"><figcaption><b>Ann</b><span>Role</span></figcaption></figure>...</div> 63 <!-- diagram --> <h2>Title</h2><figure class="dg"><svg viewBox="0 0 1680 400">...</svg></figure> <!-- see Diagrams --> 64 <!-- case --> <p class="label">Case</p><h2>Title</h2><div class="pt"><h3>History</h3><p>Summary</p></div> 65 <div class="vitals"><div class="vital" data-flag="high"><span>BP</span><b>162/94</b></div><div class="vital"><span>HR</span><b>96</b></div></div> 66 <ol class="course" data-build="list"><li><time>00:06</time>Event</li></ol> <!-- summary left; 2 to 4 vitals; timed course. data-flag marks an abnormal value --> 67 <!-- ask --> <h2>Raising a seed round</h2><div class="amount"><b data-build="count">$2.5<small>M</small></b><span>What it buys</span></div> 68 <ul class="use"><li style="--w:50"><b>Engineering</b><span>50%</span><i></i></li></ul><dl class="terms"><div><dt>Instrument</dt><dd>SAFE</dd></div></dl> 69 <!-- rows --> <h2>Title</h2><ol class="rows"><li data-k="Issue"><p>Text</p></li><li data-k="Conclusion" data-hot><h3>Bold line</h3><p>Text</p></li></ol> 70 <!-- labelled rows: issue / rule / application / conclusion; situation / complication / resolution; claim / evidence / caveat. data-hot highlights one --> 71 <!-- quiz --> <h2>Question?</h2><ol class="opts" data-build="reveal"><li>A</li><li data-correct>B</li><li>C</li><li>D</li></ol> <!-- the click marks the data-correct option --> 72 <!-- materials --> <h2>Title</h2><div class="board"><figure class="mat" style="--sw:#9a9892"><figcaption><b>Concrete</b><span>Where it goes</span></figcaption></figure>...</div> <!-- or an <img> in each figure; --tx adds a texture gradient --> 73 <!-- formula --> <h2>Title</h2><div class="eq"><i>P<sub>r</sub></i> = <i>P<sub>t</sub></i> − <span class="hot"><i>L</i></span></div><dl class="terms"><div><dt><i>P<sub>t</sub></i></dt><dd>Meaning</dd></div></dl> 74 <!-- two-column x3 -> add data-cols="3" to the section for three columns (now / next / later) --> 75 <!-- closing --> <h2>Thank you</h2><p class="contact"><span><b>Web</b> example.com</span><span>me@example.com</span></p> 76 ``` 77 78 Extras: `<p class="label">` is the small mono kicker above a title (use it on some slides, not all). `.chip` is a boxed token; `.chip.hot` 79 highlights one. `.lede`, `.src` and `<small>` are secondary text. `data-footer="off"` hides the footer, `data-fit="off"` stops auto-fit, 80 `data-tone="hero"` (or `"plain"`) swaps a slide into (or out of) the theme's hero palette. 81 82 ## 3. Deck recipes (theme, fonts, sequence, builds) 83 84 Fonts: `data-fonts` is optional; leave it empty to use the theme's own pairing. 85 86 | Need | Theme | Sequence of layouts | Builds | 87 |---|---|---|---| 88 | **Product launch** | `keynote-black` (cinematic) or `keynote-white` | title, statement, statement + big-number (Magic Move on the number), stats, full-bleed, image-left, chart or comparison, quote, timeline, closing | `count` on stats, `list` on timeline, magic on the hero number | 89 | **Quarterly / board review** | `boardroom` | title, agenda, big-number, chart (actual vs plan), stats, chart (line with `data-min`), section, comparison (mark `rec`), two-column (risks / mitigations), timeline, bullets (decisions), closing | `count` on KPIs, `draw` on charts, `list` on decisions | 90 | **Tech talk** | `swiss` (or `studio`) | title, statement + big-number (problem), diagram (before), section, diagram (after), process, code (`data-focus`), chart (line), comparison, two-column (worked / didn't), stats, closing | `draw` + `fade` on diagram groups, focus on code | 91 | **Training / course** | `studio` (or `editorial`) | title, agenda, statement, diagrams, process, big-number, chart, comparison, code, quote, timeline (where we are), closing | `list`, `draw`, one `count` | 92 | **Investor pitch** | `keynote-white` + `data-fonts="grotesk"` | title, statement (problem), big-number (market), image-left (solution), stats (traction), chart (growth), comparison (vs alternatives), team, timeline (use of funds), closing | `count` on traction, `draw` on the growth chart | 93 | **Weekly status update** | `editorial` or `keynote-white` | title, bullets (done), stats (health), chart (trend), timeline (next), two-column (risks / asks), closing | `list` only; keep it quiet | 94 95 Authoring order that works in one pass: write the title and the one-sentence story, pick the recipe, write each slide's single 96 claim as its `<h2>`, then add the supporting snippet, then notes, then run `check.mjs`. 97 98 ## 4. Theme design plans (DESIGN.md format) 99 100 Each theme is a real, shippable look. One accent, hairline rules, big type. All body text is at least 4.5:1. 101 102 ### keynote-white 103 - **Overview.** Apple-clean. Mostly white, enormous tightly-tracked headlines, one blue phrase per slide. Fits launches, pitches, status decks. 104 - **Colors.** bg `#ffffff`, surface `#f5f5f7`, ink `#1d1d1f`, ink2 `#5f5f64`, rule `#d2d2d7`, brand `#0066cc` (on-brand `#fff`), hero = same as page. 105 - **Typography.** Display and body Inter (700 display, -0.035em), mono JetBrains Mono for labels and code. 106 - **Shape.** Radius 14 px (panels), 6 px bars, 1 px rules. 107 - **Signature.** Whitespace and scale; the accent `<em>` is the only colour on a title. 108 - **Do / Don't.** Do keep slides sparse. Don't add boxes around everything. 109 110 ### keynote-black 111 - **Overview.** Cinematic dark for reveals and demos; the same system on pure black. 112 - **Colors.** bg `#000`, surface `#161618`, ink `#f5f5f7`, ink2 `#a1a1a6`, rule `#38383a`, brand `#2997ff`, em gradient `#2997ff` to `#c58bff`. 113 - **Typography.** Inter 700 display; JetBrains Mono. 114 - **Shape.** 14 px radius, 6 px bars. 115 - **Signature.** Gradient-filled headline accent, the only gradient in the system. Code panel `#1c1c1e` with Xcode-dark colours. 116 - **Do / Don't.** Do use for rooms with dim light. Don't print it (use keynote-white for PDF handouts). 117 118 ### boardroom 119 - **Overview.** PowerPoint-corporate done well: navy, serif titles, gold accent, rules above the footer. 120 - **Colors.** bg `#fff`, surface `#eef1f6`, ink `#0b2545`, ink2 `#46576f`, rule `#c8d0dc`, brand `#c19a3d` (text version `#7a5a0a`); hero bg navy `#0b2545` with gold `#e2b658`. 121 - **Typography.** Source Serif 4 (600) titles, Source Sans 3 body, JetBrains Mono. 122 - **Shape.** 2 px radius, square bars, 1 px rules. 123 - **Signature.** Gold spine on title and closing slides; gold left bar on every title; navy code panel. 124 - **Do / Don't.** Do put the decision on the last slide. Don't use more than one chart per slide. 125 126 ### swiss 127 - **Overview.** International typographic style: hard grid, black rules, one red. 128 - **Colors.** bg `#fff`, surface `#f0f0f0`, ink `#111`, ink2 `#555`, rule `#cfcfcf`, strong rule `#111`, brand `#d7000f`; hero slides are solid red with white type. 129 - **Typography.** Inter Tight 700 (-0.03em) display, Inter body, JetBrains Mono. 130 - **Shape.** Zero radius everywhere, 2 px black rule above the footer. 131 - **Signature.** A 96x20 red tab on the top margin and full-red hero slides. 132 - **Do / Don't.** Do align everything to the grid. Don't round corners. 133 134 ### editorial 135 - **Overview.** A printed essay: paper, ink, oxblood, italic emphasis. 136 - **Colors.** bg `#f4efe6`, surface `#ebe4d6`, ink `#1c1a17`, ink2 `#5a5347`, rule `#cfc5b2`, brand `#8f2d17`; hero is ink `#1c1a17` with terracotta `#e49467`. 137 - **Typography.** Newsreader 400 display (italic for `<em>`), Inter body, JetBrains Mono. 138 - **Shape.** Zero radius, 1 px rules. 139 - **Signature.** A masthead double rule across the top of every slide. 140 - **Do / Don't.** Do write full sentences as titles. Don't use all-caps. 141 142 ### studio 143 - **Overview.** Deep teal and amber, the look of the Wireless 101 courses: for teaching and talks. 144 - **Colors.** bg `#0a2a2f`, surface `#0f3a40`, ink `#efe8d8`, ink2 `#a9c0bd`, rule `#2c5a5f`, brand `#f0a93b` (on-brand `#0a2a2f`); hero `#061c20`. 145 - **Typography.** Instrument Serif display (italic amber `<em>`), DM Sans body, Space Mono labels. 146 - **Shape.** 4 px radius, 2 px bars. 147 - **Signature.** An amber dot starts every label. 148 - **Do / Don't.** Do keep diagrams to the amber and cream. Don't add a second accent. 149 150 Press **S** in any deck to switch theme and font pairing live; hovering an option previews it on the slide, a click keeps it (remembered per deck in localStorage). 151 152 **Font library** (9 core pairings below live in the template; the profession pairings live in `library/fonts/` and are copied into a deck with `tools/add-look.mjs`. The settings panel groups them as Core and Library, and picking a library theme selects its own pairing; `fonts.html` shows them all as specimens with your own headline): Inter (neo-grotesk), Sora/Inter (geometric), Space Grotesk/Inter (grotesk with character), IBM Plex Sans/Plex Mono (technical), Fraunces/Inter, Playfair/Source Sans, 153 Spectral/Public Sans, Cormorant Garamond/Source Sans (set at 1.15x via `--display-scale`), and system fonts. Type sizes come from one scale: `--t-display --t-h1 --t-h2 --t-h3 --t-body --t-small` (164/132/84/48/36/28 px; 28 px is the floor for anything the audience reads). 154 Set one with `data-fonts="sora"` on `<html>`. To recolour any theme, add one line: `html{--brand:#7c3aed;--brand-text:#7c3aed}`. 155 156 ## 5. Builds, transitions, Magic Move 157 158 **Builds** reveal parts of a slide one click at a time. Right arrow / space / click reveals the next build, then the next slide; left steps back. 159 160 | Attribute | Effect | 161 |---|---| 162 | `data-build="fade"`, `rise`, `scale`, `wipe` | the element appears | 163 | `data-build="list"` on a `ul`/`ol` | children appear one by one (`data-item="fade"` to change the style) | 164 | `data-build="draw"` on an SVG shape or `<g>` | strokes draw themselves (every shape inside is staggered) | 165 | `data-build="count"` | the number counts up from 0 (`$4.2M`, `38.4%`, `1,840` all work); markup holds the final value | 166 | `data-build="draw"` on a chart figure | bars grow, lines draw, labels arrive | 167 | `data-focus="1-3;5-7;*"` on a `pre` | each click lights the next range of lines (`*` = all) | 168 | `data-order="2"` | builds with the same order arrive together; give all builds an order or none | 169 | `data-delay="200"` | extra delay in ms | 170 171 Print, overview thumbnails and `check.mjs` always show every build; the presenter window's Next pane shows the next one. Charts take `data-target="200"` (a dashed target line), `data-delta="pct"` or `"abs"` (a delta label on two-series columns), `data-muted="2"` (which series is the muted reference; with two bar series the second is one by default, `data-equal` turns that off) and `data-highlight` (also on line charts). Chart data is exposed to screen readers as a hidden table. Use builds where order matters; most slides need none. 172 173 **Skip, appendix and the end.** `data-skip` on a slide keeps it in the overview, outline and PDF but jumps over it in play (Keynote's Skip Slide); use it for backup slides. A slide with `data-layout="appendix"` renders as a section divider and it and every slide after it are skipped in play. Pressing next on the last slide shows an "End of show" screen (`data-end="off"` on the deck turns it off). Cite sources with `<sup class="cite">[1]</sup>` and list them on a `references` slide (`<ol class="refs"><li><div><cite>Title</cite> <span>Detail</span></div></li></ol>`). Recipes: an agenda that returns at each section break, with `aria-current` on the current item; a Q&A slide is a `closing` slide whose label says Questions. 174 175 **Transitions.** Default is a quick dissolve. `data-transition="push"`, `"move-in"` or `"none"` per slide (the incoming slide's setting wins). 176 177 **Magic Move.** Give an element on one slide and an element on the next the same `data-magic="id"` and they morph: position, size, colour, 178 opacity. If the typeface differs between the two (sentence to chip, serif to mono) it cross-fades while it travels. It works on text, boxes 179 and SVG; use a `<span>` rather than `<em>` for text that changes colour. A slide pair with no shared ids just dissolves. 180 181 ## 6. Diagrams that draw 182 183 Author the SVG with `viewBox="0 0 1680 H"` (so 1 unit is 1 px at full width) and use the engine classes so it follows the theme: 184 `dg-box` (outline), `dg-hot` (accent outline), `dg-line` and `dg-line hot`, `dg-dot`, text classes `dg-t` (label), `dg-s` (small), `dg-m` (mono), `dg-b` (accent). 185 Wrap groups in `<g data-build="fade" data-order="1">` for boxes and `<g data-build="draw" data-order="2">` for arrows (stroke-only paths, arrowheads as part of 186 the path). Crop the viewBox to the content (`viewBox="0 150 1680 330"`) so the diagram fills the slide. See `examples/src/gen_diagrams.py` for generators. 187 188 ## 6b. Images 189 190 Photos and illustrations go in `<img>` inside `image-left`, `image-right`, `team`, or as `data-bg` / `<img class="bleed">` on `full-bleed` (cropped with `object-fit: cover`, scrim added for legibility). 191 Always give `alt` text. Re-encode photos without EXIF/GPS (Pillow: open, convert, save; `sips` alone keeps metadata). 192 193 Local generation (nothing leaves the machine): `tools/gen-images.sh` renders the illustrations in `assets/` with the Draw Things CLI (`z_image_turbo`), strips metadata through Pillow and 194 writes JPEGs of about 70 to 110 KB; `tools/gen-images.sh name "prompt" seed WxH` renders one more. Rules that came from the Wireless 101 pipeline: generated images are **illustrative only**; never ask 195 for text, numbers, charts or diagrams (models garble them, so those stay SVG); no real people or brands; judge each render and drop the bad ones. 196 The four examples use `assets/aria-hero.jpg`, `aria-market.jpg` and `warehouse.jpg`; `abstract-teal.jpg` is a spare for dark decks. 197 198 ## 7. Presenter keys and tools 199 200 | Key | Action | 201 |---|---| 202 | right, down, space, PageDown, N, click | next build / slide | 203 | left, up, PageUp, Backspace, Shift+space | previous | 204 | Home / End | first / last slide | 205 | number + Enter | jump to slide (a toast shows what you typed; works in the presenter window too) | 206 | **G** | overview (light table; arrows move, Enter opens). **Esc** only closes panels, the overview, the laser or the marker; it never opens anything, so a clicker's Esc cannot put the grid on the projector | 207 | **P** | presenter view in a new window (this is the presenter view, not PDF export): current slide, a Next pane that previews the next build (or the next slide when builds are done), notes (A- / A+ or + / - change their size), timer (click or T pauses; `data-duration="20"` on the deck makes it a countdown that turns amber for the last two minutes), clock, an AUDIENCE SCREEN badge when the projector is blanked. Every key above works there too, and it reconnects if the audience window is reloaded (allow pop-ups) | 208 | **M** | marker: draw on the slide with mouse, pen or finger. **1 2 3 4** red / yellow / blue / white, **H** highlighter, **E** eraser, **Ctrl/Cmd+Z** undo, **C** clear, **Esc** leave. Kept per slide, remembered per deck in localStorage, shown in the presenter window, never printed | 209 | **L** | laser pointer: a red dot follows the mouse and leaves no trace | 210 | **O** | outline: every slide with title, link, layout, build count, notes flag; click to jump, filter, Copy as text; `#` copies one slide's link, Links copies them all | 211 | **K** | copy a link to this slide (also the link button in the toolbar) | 212 | **A** | narration on/off, when the deck has `data-narration` clips (see 12a) | 213 | **S** | theme and font panel; hover or focus a theme or pairing to preview it live on the slide, click to keep it | 214 | **B** or **.** / **W** | black / white screen | 215 | **F** or **F5** | fullscreen (F5 so a clicker's start button does not reload the page) | 216 217 The toolbar at the bottom fades when idle (and the cursor hides). Every slide has a link: `deck.html#pricing`, from `data-id="pricing"` on the section, else from its title, else `#slide-7` (`#/7` and `#7` work too); the address bar follows the current slide. Touch: swipe left/right; tap the 218 left 22% to go back (the rest advances); the toolbar stays visible while it has keyboard focus. `prefers-reduced-motion` is honoured in JS: no transitions, builds appear instantly, counters show the final value. 219 220 ## 8. PDF and print 221 222 Open the deck in Chrome, **Cmd/Ctrl+P**, destination "Save as PDF", margins "None", turn on "Background graphics". `@page` is 1920x1080 px, one slide per 223 page, all builds shown, backgrounds kept, toolbar and marker hidden. Headless: `page.pdf({preferCSSPageSize: true, printBackground: true})`. 224 225 ## 9. Right-to-left and Arabic 226 227 Set `dir="rtl" lang="ar"` on `<html>` (the lang drives chart number formatting: Arabic-Indic digits for `ar`, and `data-build="count"` accepts Arabic-Indic digits) or on a single `<section>`. See `examples/arabic-sample.html`. Serif themes carry `--f-ar-d` (Noto Naskh Arabic) for Arabic headings; Arabic headings get line-height 1.25. All layout uses logical properties, so slides mirror (image-left becomes right, timelines run 228 right to left, the wipe direction flips). An Arabic face loads on demand. Keep code in `dir="ltr"` blocks (the code layout already is). 229 230 ## 10. Checker 231 232 ``` 233 node check.mjs deck.html [more.html] [--themes] [--shots out/] [--outline] 234 ``` 235 236 Opens each deck at 1920x1080, shows every slide with all builds revealed and prints a short list: `slide n: element, what is wrong, fix:`. It reports 237 content outside the safe area (120 px sides, 96 px top/bottom) or the slide, text wider than its box, text under 20 px, text contrast under 4.5:1 (including 238 gradient-filled headline accents), and console errors. Exit code 1 on failure; a 15-slide deck takes about 2 seconds. `--themes` repeats the run in every 239 theme the deck defines (use it before sending a deck to someone who might press S). `--shots` saves a PNG per slide. `--outline` prints the deck's outline (n, title, layout, builds, magic, and `NO NOTES` where notes are missing), handy for reviewing a generated deck without opening it. 240 241 Needs Playwright: `npm i playwright && npx playwright install chromium`. Or set `PLAYWRIGHT_MODULE=/path/to/playwright/index.mjs` and 242 `CHROME_PATH=/path/to/chrome`. 243 244 ## 12. Checklist before you present 245 246 - `node check.mjs deck.html --themes` is green. 247 - Press **G**: the sequence reads as a story; every slide has one claim. 248 - Press **P**: notes on every slide that needs one; the timer works. 249 - Try the Magic Move pairs and the builds once in presentation order. 250 - Print to PDF and look at page 1, the chart page and the last page. 251 - Open with the system's reduced-motion setting on if your audience may need it. 252 253 ## 12a. Narration (recorded voice per slide) 254 255 Add `data-narration="audio/my-deck/"` to `<main class="deck">` and put one MP3 per slide in that folder, named after the 256 slide's link id (`data-id`, for example `audio/my-deck/pricing.mp3`). A speaker button appears in the toolbar once the first 257 slide's clip loads (key **A**, also from the presenter window). While narration is on, each slide plays its clip, shows all 258 its builds, and moves to the next slide when the clip ends; navigating by hand keeps narrating from where you land. 259 Until the files exist the deck shows no button at all, so a deck can ship first and get its voice later. 260 261 ## 12b. Slides that run 262 263 A slide is a web page, so it can hold things a slide file can't: a working app screen, a calculator, a simulation you drag, 264 sound and speech, code you edit and run, a game, another page in an iframe, a video that plays only on its slide, a live camera. 265 `examples/beyond-slides.html` has one of each; its source (`examples/src/beyond-slides.html`) is the pattern to copy: 266 wrap widgets in `.bx-ui` (clicks there don't advance), take colours from the theme tokens, and run anything that moves or 267 makes sound only while the slide is current. The video in it (`assets/edit-in-browser.mp4`) is a recording of `editor.html`. 268 269 ## 13. Known limits 270 271 - Web fonts come from Google Fonts on demand; offline, the system fallbacks in each stack are used (set `data-fonts="system"` for fully offline decks). 272 - Charts are simple on purpose: column, bar and line, up to three series, no stacked or dual-axis. 273 - Magic Move morphs matching elements; it does not morph SVG path shapes into different paths. 274 - The presenter view needs pop-ups allowed and uses `postMessage`, so both windows must stay open. 275 - The engine fits type by shrinking to 78% (display numbers and headlines to 50%); below that the checker reports the slide instead of shrinking further. 276 277 <!-- LIBRARY:START (generated by tools/build-gallery.mjs from tools/library-data.mjs; edit the data file) --> 278

file.content: # Keynote Pro manual (the engine behind present-in-html) Paths below are the engine's. In this skill: `check.mjs` and `tools/*.mjs` are in `scripts/`; `template.html`, `library/` and `examples/` are in `assets/`. Build tools and the sample decks mentioned here are not shipped with the skill. - 1. Write a deck in 60 seconds - 2. Layout cheat-sheet (shortest working snippet for each) - 3. Deck recipes (theme, fonts, sequence, builds) - 4. Theme design plans (DESIGN.md format) - 5. Builds, transitions, Magic Move - 6. Diagrams that draw - 6b. Images - 7. Presenter keys and tools - 8. PDF and print - 9. Right-to-left and Arabic - 10. Checker - 12. Checklist before you present - 12a. Narration (recorded voice per slide) - 12b. Slides that run - 13. Known limits ## 1. Write a deck in 60 seconds 1. Copy `template.html`. Set `data-theme` (and optionally `data-fonts`) on ``, and the title in `` and `data-title` on `<main class="deck">`. 2. Delete the sample slides. Add `<section class="slide" data-layout="...">` blocks (cheat-sheet below). 3. Add `<aside class="notes"><p>...</p></aside>` inside any slide for presenter notes. 4. `node check.mjs my-deck.html`, fix what it lists, open it, press **P**. Rules of thumb: one idea per slide; at most 5 bullets; say the number, not the paragraph. Layouts auto-fit (type shrinks to 78% before content would leave the safe area, and short content grows, up to 1.25x on bullets and 1.5x on statements, so a slide is never half empty), lists balance their wrapping, images crop with `object-fit: cover`. You never tune CSS to make text fit; if `check.mjs` still complains, cut words. ## 2. Layout cheat-sheet (shortest working snippet for each) Every snippet goes inside `<section class="slide" data-layout="NAME"> ... </section>`. Optional extras are in comments. ```html <!-- title --> <h1>Title with <em>one accent</em></h1><p class="sub">Subtitle</p> <!-- <p class="label">Event</p> <p class="meta"><span>Name</span><span>Date</span></p> --> <!-- section --> <h2>Part two</h2> <!-- <p class="label">Part two</p> <span class="num">2</span> <p>One-line promise</p> --> <!-- statement --> <h2>One huge sentence with an <em>accent</em>.</h2> <!-- agenda --> <h2>Agenda</h2><ol><li>Results <small>10 min</small></li><li>Plan</li></ol> <!-- aria-current on an li dims the rest --> <!-- bullets --> <h2>Title</h2><ul data-build="list"><li><strong>Lead.</strong> Support.</li><li>Two</li><li>Three</li></ul> <!-- two-column --> <h2>Title</h2><div class="col"><h3>A</h3><p>Text</p></div><div class="col"><h3>B</h3><ul><li>x</li></ul></div> <!-- image-left --> <figure><img src="a.jpg" alt=""></figure><h2>Title</h2><p>Text</p> <!-- empty <figure></figure> = placeholder art --> <!-- image-right --> (same markup, mirrored) <!-- full-bleed --> <h2>Title on a photo</h2> <!-- data-bg="photo.jpg" on the section, or <img class="bleed" src alt=""> --> <!-- big-number --> <div class="big" data-build="count">98<small>%</small></div><p>One honest caption.</p> <!-- <p class="src">Source</p> --> <!-- stats --> <h2>Title</h2><div class="stat"><b>4.2M</b><span>Users</span></div> ...2 to 4 of these <!-- chart --> <h2>Title</h2><p class="lede">Takeaway</p> <figure class="chart" data-chart="column" data-values="Q1:12,Q2:18,Q3:21"></figure> <!-- data-chart: column | bar | line. Multi-series: put a <table> inside (header row + label column). data-prefix="$" data-unit="M" data-decimals="1" data-highlight="3" (1-based or a label) data-min="92" (line charts only) data-build="draw" (bars grow, lines draw) data-wide on the section = full-width plot; <figcaption>Source</figcaption> --> <!-- comparison --> <h2>Title</h2><table><thead><tr><th></th><th>A</th><th class="rec" data-tag="Recommended">B</th></tr></thead> <tbody><tr><th>Price</th><td>$1</td><td>$2</td></tr></tbody></table> <!-- timeline --> <h2>Title</h2><ol class="timeline" data-build="list"><li><time>Q1</time><h3>Step</h3><p>Detail</p></li>...</ol> <!-- class="now" marks today --> <!-- process --> <h2>Title</h2><ol class="steps" data-build="list"><li><h3>Capture</h3><p>Detail</p></li>...</ol> <!-- 3 to 5 steps --> <!-- quote --> <blockquote>The quote with an <em>accent</em>.</blockquote><cite><b>Name</b>Title, Company</cite> <!-- code --> <h2>Title</h2><pre data-lang="js" data-focus="1-2;4-6;*"> code </pre> <!-- indent freely; focus steps light lines per click --> <!-- team --> <h2>Team</h2><div class="people"><figure class="person" data-initials="AK"><figcaption><b>Ann</b><span>Role</span></figcaption></figure>...</div> <!-- diagram --> <h2>Title</h2><figure class="dg"><svg viewBox="0 0 1680 400">...</svg></figure> <!-- see Diagrams --> <!-- case --> <p class="label">Case</p><h2>Title</h2><div class="pt"><h3>History</h3><p>Summary</p></div> <div class="vitals"><div class="vital" data-flag="high"><span>BP</span><b>162/94</b></div><div class="vital"><span>HR</span><b>96</b></div></div> <ol class="course" data-build="list"><li><time>00:06</time>Event</li></ol> <!-- summary left; 2 to 4 vitals; timed course. data-flag marks an abnormal value --> <!-- ask --> <h2>Raising a seed round</h2><div class="amount"><b data-build="count">$2.5<small>M</small></b><span>What it buys</span></div> <ul class="use"><li style="--w:50"><b>Engineering</b><span>50%</span><i></i></li></ul><dl class="terms"><div><dt>Instrument</dt><dd>SAFE</dd></div></dl> <!-- rows --> <h2>Title</h2><ol class="rows"><li data-k="Issue"><p>Text</p></li><li data-k="Conclusion" data-hot><h3>Bold line</h3><p>Text</p></li></ol> <!-- labelled rows: issue / rule / application / conclusion; situation / complication / resolution; claim / evidence / caveat. data-hot highlights one --> <!-- quiz --> <h2>Question?</h2><ol class="opts" data-build="reveal"><li>A</li><li data-correct>B</li><li>C</li><li>D</li></ol> <!-- the click marks the data-correct option --> <!-- materials --> <h2>Title</h2><div class="board"><figure class="mat" style="--sw:#9a9892"><figcaption><b>Concrete</b><span>Where it goes</span></figcaption></figure>...</div> <!-- or an <img> in each figure; --tx adds a texture gradient --> <!-- formula --> <h2>Title</h2><div class="eq"><i>P<sub>r</sub></i> = <i>P<sub>t</sub></i> − <span class="hot"><i>L</i></span></div><dl class="terms"><div><dt><i>P<sub>t</sub></i></dt><dd>Meaning</dd></div></dl> <!-- two-column x3 -> add data-cols="3" to the section for three columns (now / next / later) --> <!-- closing --> <h2>Thank you</h2><p class="contact"><span><b>Web</b> example.com</span><span>me@example.com</span></p> ``` Extras: `<p class="label">` is the small mono kicker above a title (use it on some slides, not all). `.chip` is a boxed token; `.chip.hot` highlights one. `.lede`, `.src` and `<small>` are secondary text. `data-footer="off"` hides the footer, `data-fit="off"` stops auto-fit, `data-tone="hero"` (or `"plain"`) swaps a slide into (or out of) the theme's hero palette. ## 3. Deck recipes (theme, fonts, sequence, builds) Fonts: `data-fonts` is optional; leave it empty to use the theme's own pairing. | Need | Theme | Sequence of layouts | Builds | |---|---|---|---| | **Product launch** | `keynote-black` (cinematic) or `keynote-white` | title, statement, statement + big-number (Magic Move on the number), stats, full-bleed, image-left, chart or comparison, quote, timeline, closing | `count` on stats, `list` on timeline, magic on the hero number | | **Quarterly / board review** | `boardroom` | title, agenda, big-number, chart (actual vs plan), stats, chart (line with `data-min`), section, comparison (mark `rec`), two-column (risks / mitigations), timeline, bullets (decisions), closing | `count` on KPIs, `draw` on charts, `list` on decisions | | **Tech talk** | `swiss` (or `studio`) | title, statement + big-number (problem), diagram (before), section, diagram (after), process, code (`data-focus`), chart (line), comparison, two-column (worked / didn't), stats, closing | `draw` + `fade` on diagram groups, focus on code | | **Training / course** | `studio` (or `editorial`) | title, agenda, statement, diagrams, process, big-number, chart, comparison, code, quote, timeline (where we are), closing | `list`, `draw`, one `count` | | **Investor pitch** | `keynote-white` + `data-fonts="grotesk"` | title, statement (problem), big-number (market), image-left (solution), stats (traction), chart (growth), comparison (vs alternatives), team, timeline (use of funds), closing | `count` on traction, `draw` on the growth chart | | **Weekly status update** | `editorial` or `keynote-white` | title, bullets (done), stats (health), chart (trend), timeline (next), two-column (risks / asks), closing | `list` only; keep it quiet | Authoring order that works in one pass: write the title and the one-sentence story, pick the recipe, write each slide's single claim as its `<h2>`, then add the supporting snippet, then notes, then run `check.mjs`. ## 4. Theme design plans (DESIGN.md format) Each theme is a real, shippable look. One accent, hairline rules, big type. All body text is at least 4.5:1. ### keynote-white - **Overview.** Apple-clean. Mostly white, enormous tightly-tracked headlines, one blue phrase per slide. Fits launches, pitches, status decks. - **Colors.** bg `#ffffff`, surface `#f5f5f7`, ink `#1d1d1f`, ink2 `#5f5f64`, rule `#d2d2d7`, brand `#0066cc` (on-brand `#fff`), hero = same as page. - **Typography.** Display and body Inter (700 display, -0.035em), mono JetBrains Mono for labels and code. - **Shape.** Radius 14 px (panels), 6 px bars, 1 px rules. - **Signature.** Whitespace and scale; the accent `<em>` is the only colour on a title. - **Do / Don't.** Do keep slides sparse. Don't add boxes around everything. ### keynote-black - **Overview.** Cinematic dark for reveals and demos; the same system on pure black. - **Colors.** bg `#000`, surface `#161618`, ink `#f5f5f7`, ink2 `#a1a1a6`, rule `#38383a`, brand `#2997ff`, em gradient `#2997ff` to `#c58bff`. - **Typography.** Inter 700 display; JetBrains Mono. - **Shape.** 14 px radius, 6 px bars. - **Signature.** Gradient-filled headline accent, the only gradient in the system. Code panel `#1c1c1e` with Xcode-dark colours. - **Do / Don't.** Do use for rooms with dim light. Don't print it (use keynote-white for PDF handouts). ### boardroom - **Overview.** PowerPoint-corporate done well: navy, serif titles, gold accent, rules above the footer. - **Colors.** bg `#fff`, surface `#eef1f6`, ink `#0b2545`, ink2 `#46576f`, rule `#c8d0dc`, brand `#c19a3d` (text version `#7a5a0a`); hero bg navy `#0b2545` with gold `#e2b658`. - **Typography.** Source Serif 4 (600) titles, Source Sans 3 body, JetBrains Mono. - **Shape.** 2 px radius, square bars, 1 px rules. - **Signature.** Gold spine on title and closing slides; gold left bar on every title; navy code panel. - **Do / Don't.** Do put the decision on the last slide. Don't use more than one chart per slide. ### swiss - **Overview.** International typographic style: hard grid, black rules, one red. - **Colors.** bg `#fff`, surface `#f0f0f0`, ink `#111`, ink2 `#555`, rule `#cfcfcf`, strong rule `#111`, brand `#d7000f`; hero slides are solid red with white type. - **Typography.** Inter Tight 700 (-0.03em) display, Inter body, JetBrains Mono. - **Shape.** Zero radius everywhere, 2 px black rule above the footer. - **Signature.** A 96x20 red tab on the top margin and full-red hero slides. - **Do / Don't.** Do align everything to the grid. Don't round corners. ### editorial - **Overview.** A printed essay: paper, ink, oxblood, italic emphasis. - **Colors.** bg `#f4efe6`, surface `#ebe4d6`, ink `#1c1a17`, ink2 `#5a5347`, rule `#cfc5b2`, brand `#8f2d17`; hero is ink `#1c1a17` with terracotta `#e49467`. - **Typography.** Newsreader 400 display (italic for `<em>`), Inter body, JetBrains Mono. - **Shape.** Zero radius, 1 px rules. - **Signature.** A masthead double rule across the top of every slide. - **Do / Don't.** Do write full sentences as titles. Don't use all-caps. ### studio - **Overview.** Deep teal and amber, the look of the Wireless 101 courses: for teaching and talks. - **Colors.** bg `#0a2a2f`, surface `#0f3a40`, ink `#efe8d8`, ink2 `#a9c0bd`, rule `#2c5a5f`, brand `#f0a93b` (on-brand `#0a2a2f`); hero `#061c20`. - **Typography.** Instrument Serif display (italic amber `<em>`), DM Sans body, Space Mono labels. - **Shape.** 4 px radius, 2 px bars. - **Signature.** An amber dot starts every label. - **Do / Don't.** Do keep diagrams to the amber and cream. Don't add a second accent. Press **S** in any deck to switch theme and font pairing live; hovering an option previews it on the slide, a click keeps it (remembered per deck in localStorage). **Font library** (9 core pairings below live in the template; the profession pairings live in `library/fonts/` and are copied into a deck with `tools/add-look.mjs`. The settings panel groups them as Core and Library, and picking a library theme selects its own pairing; `fonts.html` shows them all as specimens with your own headline): Inter (neo-grotesk), Sora/Inter (geometric), Space Grotesk/Inter (grotesk with character), IBM Plex Sans/Plex Mono (technical), Fraunces/Inter, Playfair/Source Sans, Spectral/Public Sans, Cormorant Garamond/Source Sans (set at 1.15x via `--display-scale`), and system fonts. Type sizes come from one scale: `--t-display --t-h1 --t-h2 --t-h3 --t-body --t-small` (164/132/84/48/36/28 px; 28 px is the floor for anything the audience reads). Set one with `data-fonts="sora"` on `<html>`. To recolour any theme, add one line: `html{--brand:#7c3aed;--brand-text:#7c3aed}`. ## 5. Builds, transitions, Magic Move **Builds** reveal parts of a slide one click at a time. Right arrow / space / click reveals the next build, then the next slide; left steps back. | Attribute | Effect | |---|---| | `data-build="fade"`, `rise`, `scale`, `wipe` | the element appears | | `data-build="list"` on a `ul`/`ol` | children appear one by one (`data-item="fade"` to change the style) | | `data-build="draw"` on an SVG shape or `<g>` | strokes draw themselves (every shape inside is staggered) | | `data-build="count"` | the number counts up from 0 (`$4.2M`, `38.4%`, `1,840` all work); markup holds the final value | | `data-build="draw"` on a chart figure | bars grow, lines draw, labels arrive | | `data-focus="1-3;5-7;*"` on a `pre` | each click lights the next range of lines (`*` = all) | | `data-order="2"` | builds with the same order arrive together; give all builds an order or none | | `data-delay="200"` | extra delay in ms | Print, overview thumbnails and `check.mjs` always show every build; the presenter window's Next pane shows the next one. Charts take `data-target="200"` (a dashed target line), `data-delta="pct"` or `"abs"` (a delta label on two-series columns), `data-muted="2"` (which series is the muted reference; with two bar series the second is one by default, `data-equal` turns that off) and `data-highlight` (also on line charts). Chart data is exposed to screen readers as a hidden table. Use builds where order matters; most slides need none. **Skip, appendix and the end.** `data-skip` on a slide keeps it in the overview, outline and PDF but jumps over it in play (Keynote's Skip Slide); use it for backup slides. A slide with `data-layout="appendix"` renders as a section divider and it and every slide after it are skipped in play. Pressing next on the last slide shows an "End of show" screen (`data-end="off"` on the deck turns it off). Cite sources with `<sup class="cite">[1]</sup>` and list them on a `references` slide (`<ol class="refs"><li><div><cite>Title</cite> <span>Detail</span></div></li></ol>`). Recipes: an agenda that returns at each section break, with `aria-current` on the current item; a Q&A slide is a `closing` slide whose label says Questions. **Transitions.** Default is a quick dissolve. `data-transition="push"`, `"move-in"` or `"none"` per slide (the incoming slide's setting wins). **Magic Move.** Give an element on one slide and an element on the next the same `data-magic="id"` and they morph: position, size, colour, opacity. If the typeface differs between the two (sentence to chip, serif to mono) it cross-fades while it travels. It works on text, boxes and SVG; use a `<span>` rather than `<em>` for text that changes colour. A slide pair with no shared ids just dissolves. ## 6. Diagrams that draw Author the SVG with `viewBox="0 0 1680 H"` (so 1 unit is 1 px at full width) and use the engine classes so it follows the theme: `dg-box` (outline), `dg-hot` (accent outline), `dg-line` and `dg-line hot`, `dg-dot`, text classes `dg-t` (label), `dg-s` (small), `dg-m` (mono), `dg-b` (accent). Wrap groups in `<g data-build="fade" data-order="1">` for boxes and `<g data-build="draw" data-order="2">` for arrows (stroke-only paths, arrowheads as part of the path). Crop the viewBox to the content (`viewBox="0 150 1680 330"`) so the diagram fills the slide. See `examples/src/gen_diagrams.py` for generators. ## 6b. Images Photos and illustrations go in `<img>` inside `image-left`, `image-right`, `team`, or as `data-bg` / `<img class="bleed">` on `full-bleed` (cropped with `object-fit: cover`, scrim added for legibility). Always give `alt` text. Re-encode photos without EXIF/GPS (Pillow: open, convert, save; `sips` alone keeps metadata). Local generation (nothing leaves the machine): `tools/gen-images.sh` renders the illustrations in `assets/` with the Draw Things CLI (`z_image_turbo`), strips metadata through Pillow and writes JPEGs of about 70 to 110 KB; `tools/gen-images.sh name "prompt" seed WxH` renders one more. Rules that came from the Wireless 101 pipeline: generated images are **illustrative only**; never ask for text, numbers, charts or diagrams (models garble them, so those stay SVG); no real people or brands; judge each render and drop the bad ones. The four examples use `assets/aria-hero.jpg`, `aria-market.jpg` and `warehouse.jpg`; `abstract-teal.jpg` is a spare for dark decks. ## 7. Presenter keys and tools | Key | Action | |---|---| | right, down, space, PageDown, N, click | next build / slide | | left, up, PageUp, Backspace, Shift+space | previous | | Home / End | first / last slide | | number + Enter | jump to slide (a toast shows what you typed; works in the presenter window too) | | **G** | overview (light table; arrows move, Enter opens). **Esc** only closes panels, the overview, the laser or the marker; it never opens anything, so a clicker's Esc cannot put the grid on the projector | | **P** | presenter view in a new window (this is the presenter view, not PDF export): current slide, a Next pane that previews the next build (or the next slide when builds are done), notes (A- / A+ or + / - change their size), timer (click or T pauses; `data-duration="20"` on the deck makes it a countdown that turns amber for the last two minutes), clock, an AUDIENCE SCREEN badge when the projector is blanked. Every key above works there too, and it reconnects if the audience window is reloaded (allow pop-ups) | | **M** | marker: draw on the slide with mouse, pen or finger. **1 2 3 4** red / yellow / blue / white, **H** highlighter, **E** eraser, **Ctrl/Cmd+Z** undo, **C** clear, **Esc** leave. Kept per slide, remembered per deck in localStorage, shown in the presenter window, never printed | | **L** | laser pointer: a red dot follows the mouse and leaves no trace | | **O** | outline: every slide with title, link, layout, build count, notes flag; click to jump, filter, Copy as text; `#` copies one slide's link, Links copies them all | | **K** | copy a link to this slide (also the link button in the toolbar) | | **A** | narration on/off, when the deck has `data-narration` clips (see 12a) | | **S** | theme and font panel; hover or focus a theme or pairing to preview it live on the slide, click to keep it | | **B** or **.** / **W** | black / white screen | | **F** or **F5** | fullscreen (F5 so a clicker's start button does not reload the page) | The toolbar at the bottom fades when idle (and the cursor hides). Every slide has a link: `deck.html#pricing`, from `data-id="pricing"` on the section, else from its title, else `#slide-7` (`#/7` and `#7` work too); the address bar follows the current slide. Touch: swipe left/right; tap the left 22% to go back (the rest advances); the toolbar stays visible while it has keyboard focus. `prefers-reduced-motion` is honoured in JS: no transitions, builds appear instantly, counters show the final value. ## 8. PDF and print Open the deck in Chrome, **Cmd/Ctrl+P**, destination "Save as PDF", margins "None", turn on "Background graphics". `@page` is 1920x1080 px, one slide per page, all builds shown, backgrounds kept, toolbar and marker hidden. Headless: `page.pdf({preferCSSPageSize: true, printBackground: true})`. ## 9. Right-to-left and Arabic Set `dir="rtl" lang="ar"` on `<html>` (the lang drives chart number formatting: Arabic-Indic digits for `ar`, and `data-build="count"` accepts Arabic-Indic digits) or on a single `<section>`. See `examples/arabic-sample.html`. Serif themes carry `--f-ar-d` (Noto Naskh Arabic) for Arabic headings; Arabic headings get line-height 1.25. All layout uses logical properties, so slides mirror (image-left becomes right, timelines run right to left, the wipe direction flips). An Arabic face loads on demand. Keep code in `dir="ltr"` blocks (the code layout already is). ## 10. Checker ``` node check.mjs deck.html [more.html] [--themes] [--shots out/] [--outline] ``` Opens each deck at 1920x1080, shows every slide with all builds revealed and prints a short list: `slide n: element, what is wrong, fix:`. It reports content outside the safe area (120 px sides, 96 px top/bottom) or the slide, text wider than its box, text under 20 px, text contrast under 4.5:1 (including gradient-filled headline accents), and console errors. Exit code 1 on failure; a 15-slide deck takes about 2 seconds. `--themes` repeats the run in every theme the deck defines (use it before sending a deck to someone who might press S). `--shots` saves a PNG per slide. `--outline` prints the deck's outline (n, title, layout, builds, magic, and `NO NOTES` where notes are missing), handy for reviewing a generated deck without opening it. Needs Playwright: `npm i playwright && npx playwright install chromium`. Or set `PLAYWRIGHT_MODULE=/path/to/playwright/index.mjs` and `CHROME_PATH=/path/to/chrome`. ## 12. Checklist before you present - `node check.mjs deck.html --themes` is green. - Press **G**: the sequence reads as a story; every slide has one claim. - Press **P**: notes on every slide that needs one; the timer works. - Try the Magic Move pairs and the builds once in presentation order. - Print to PDF and look at page 1, the chart page and the last page. - Open with the system's reduced-motion setting on if your audience may need it. ## 12a. Narration (recorded voice per slide) Add `data-narration="audio/my-deck/"` to `<main class="deck">` and put one MP3 per slide in that folder, named after the slide's link id (`data-id`, for example `audio/my-deck/pricing.mp3`). A speaker button appears in the toolbar once the first slide's clip loads (key **A**, also from the presenter window). While narration is on, each slide plays its clip, shows all its builds, and moves to the next slide when the clip ends; navigating by hand keeps narrating from where you land. Until the files exist the deck shows no button at all, so a deck can ship first and get its voice later. ## 12b. Slides that run A slide is a web page, so it can hold things a slide file can't: a working app screen, a calculator, a simulation you drag, sound and speech, code you edit and run, a game, another page in an iframe, a video that plays only on its slide, a live camera. `examples/beyond-slides.html` has one of each; its source (`examples/src/beyond-slides.html`) is the pattern to copy: wrap widgets in `.bx-ui` (clicks there don't advance), take colours from the theme tokens, and run anything that moves or makes sound only while the slide is current. The video in it (`assets/edit-in-browser.mp4`) is a recording of `editor.html`. ## 13. Known limits - Web fonts come from Google Fonts on demand; offline, the system fallbacks in each stack are used (set `data-fonts="system"` for fully offline decks). - Charts are simple on purpose: column, bar and line, up to three series, no stacked or dual-axis. - Magic Move morphs matching elements; it does not morph SVG path shapes into different paths. - The presenter view needs pop-ups allowed and uses `postMessage`, so both windows must stay open. - The engine fits type by shrinking to 78% (display numbers and headlines to 50%); below that the checker reports the slide instead of shrinking further. <!-- LIBRARY:START (generated by tools/build-gallery.mjs from tools/library-data.mjs; edit the data file) -->

<!doctype html>
<!--
  KEYNOTE PRO  -  one-file HTML presentation template.
  1. Copy this file.  2. Set data-theme / data-fonts on <html> and the title below.
  3. Replace the slides between SLIDES:START and SLIDES:END.  4. Open in a browser. That is all.
  Keys: arrows/space next-back, O outline, G overview (Esc only closes), P presenter view, M marker (H highlighter, Ctrl/Cmd+Z undo), L laser, S theme+fonts (hover previews), F fullscreen, B/W black/white, 12 Enter jump.
  Docs: README.md.  Engine: the <style id="kp-engine"> and <script> blocks (no dependencies; fonts load from Google on demand).
-->
<html lang="en" data-theme="keynote-white" data-fonts="">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<title>present-in-html template</title>
<style id="kp-themes">
/* =====================================================================
   THEME TOKEN CONTRACT
   A theme is ONE block: a marker comment "THEME:name | Label | swatch | fonts-url" (written as a CSS comment),
   then html[data-theme="name"]{ ... }, then a closing comment "/THEME". See the real blocks below.
   Layouts and components read ONLY these tokens (no colour, font or weight is hard-coded in layout CSS).
   Themes may add small signature rules (decorations) inside their own block, scoped by [data-theme="name"].
   The settings panel (S) lists whatever THEME / FONTS blocks exist in this <style>. Scripts can add or remove blocks.

   COLOUR (required)
     --bg --bg2          slide background, quiet panel/surface
     --ink --ink2        body text, secondary text   (>= 4.5:1 on --bg and --bg2)
     --rule              hairline colour             --rule-strong   hard rule / table head / outline colour
     --brand             the one accent (fills, bars, dots)      --brand-text  accent used as TEXT (>= 4.5:1 on --bg)
     --on-brand          text drawn on a --brand fill
   HERO SLIDES (title, section, closing, full-bleed, data-tone="hero"; required)
     --hero-bg --hero-ink --hero-ink2 --hero-rule --hero-brand
----
5:  3. Replace the slides between SLIDES:START and SLIDES:END.  4. Open in a browser. That is all.
7:  Docs: README.md.  Engine: the <style id="kp-engine"> and <script> blocks (no dependencies; fonts load from Google on demand).

420:[data-layout="diagram"] figcaption{font:var(--t-small)/1.3 var(--f-mono);color:var(--ink2);margin-top:16px}

496:[data-layout="formula"] .eq{font-family:var(--f-display);font-weight:400;font-size:calc(140px*var(--fit));line-height:1.25;letter-spacing:-0.01em;text-align:center;white-space:nowrap;padding:36px 0;margin-block:auto 44px;border-block:var(--rule-w,1px) solid var(--rule-strong)}

<!doctype html>
<!--
  KEYNOTE PRO  -  one-file HTML presentation template.
  1. Copy this file.  2. Set data-theme / data-fonts on <html> and the title below.
  3. Replace the slides between SLIDES:START and SLIDES:END.  4. Open in a browser. That is all.
  Keys: arrows/space next-back, O outline, G overview (Esc only closes), P presenter view, M marker (H highlighter, Ctrl/Cmd+Z undo), L laser, S theme+fonts (hover previews), F fullscreen, B/W black/white, 12 Enter jump.
  Docs: README.md.  Engine: the <style id="kp-engine"> and <script> blocks (no dependencies; fonts load from Google on demand).
-->
<html lang="en" data-theme="keynote-white" data-fonts="">

<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

/* =====================================================================

   A theme is ONE block: a marker comment "THEME:name | Label | swatch | fonts-url" (written as a CSS comment),

   Themes may add small signature rules (decorations) inside their own block, scoped by [data-theme="name"].
   The settings panel (S) lists whatever THEME / FONTS blocks exist in this <style>. Scripts can add or remove blocks.

     --on-brand          text drawn on a --brand fill
   HERO SLIDES (title, section, closing, full-bleed, data-tone="hero"; required)
     --hero-bg --hero-ink --hero-ink2 --hero-rule --hero-brand
----

# Wireless 101, Module 1: How Wireless Communication Works

- **Audience**: first-year undergraduates with high-school algebra and logarithms; no radio background
- **Occasion and time**: a 50-minute lecture; the deck is paced to about 45.5 minutes, leaving time for questions and the quiz
- **Goal**: students can explain a radio wave, convert frequency and wavelength, work in decibels, compute free-space path loss and a link budget, and explain modulation, Shannon's limit, multiple access and cells
- **Promise**: By the end you will be able to say how far a signal goes, how fast it can carry data, and how many users can share the air
- **Story**: every wireless system answers three questions (how far, how fast, how many), and the same physics sets all three answers
- **Fence**: a stronger signal is not the same as a higher gain. Antenna gain focuses power into a beam; it creates no energy
- **Look**: `data-theme="spectrum"` (library look for electrical and wireless engineering, with formula and diagram layouts); `data-fonts` left empty so the theme's own pairing (`plexcond`) is used; English, left to right
- **Sources**: `wireless-101-module-1.md` (this folder), all sections
- **Placeholders**: presenter name and date on the title slide; two photos (antenna and urban street) are image placeholders with captions

| # | data-id | layout | claim (the slide's h2) | content and facts (with source) | role | min |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | start | title | How Wireless Communication Works | Subtitle = the promise; course and presenter placeholders (module intro) | promise | 0.5 |
| 2 | agenda | agenda | Every wireless system answers three questions | How far, how fast, how many; the three parts of the module (module section 1) | signpost | 1 |
| 3 | history | timeline | From Maxwell's equations to 5G took more than a century | 1865 Maxwell; 1886–88 Hertz; 1901 Marconi; 1979–83 1G; 1997 Wi-Fi 802.11; 2019 first 5G (module section 2) | story | 1.5 |
| 4 | wavelength | formula | Wavelength is the speed of light divided by frequency | λ = c / f, c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s; 100 MHz gives 3 m; 2.4 GHz gives 12.5 cm (section 3) | evidence | 2 |
| 5 | wave | diagram | A radio wave is an oscillating electric and magnetic field | Animated sine wave with one wavelength bracketed; c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s (section 3) | thesis | 2 |
| 6 | spectrum | diagram | The spectrum runs from 3 kHz to 300 GHz | ITU bands VLF to EHF with example uses; trade-off line: low frequencies go far with little bandwidth, high frequencies carry bandwidth but reach less far (section 4) | fence | 2 |
| 7 | decibels | formula | Decibels turn multiplying gains into adding them | dB = 10·log₁₀(P₂/P₁); dBm = 10·log₁₀(P/1 mW); dBi (section 5) | evidence | 2 |
| 8 | rules | stats | Three rules of thumb cover most link arithmetic | +3 dB ≈ double; +10 dB = ten times; 0 dBm = 1 mW (section 5) | story | 2 |
| 9 | antennas | image-right | Antenna gain focuses power; it does not create it | Antenna converts current to wave and back; isotropic 0 dBi; half-wave dipole 2.15 dBi; directional vs omnidirectional (section 6). Image placeholder: antennas of different types | fence | 1.5 |
| 10 | fspl | formula | Free-space path loss grows with distance and frequency | FSPL (dB) = 20·log₁₀(d) + 20·log₁₀(f) + 32.44, d in km, f in MHz; doubling distance or frequency adds about 6 dB (section 7) | evidence | 2 |
| 11 | fspl-number | big-number | Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz over 100 m loses about 80 dB | Worked example: −20.0 + 67.6 + 32.44 ≈ 80 dB (section 7) | evidence | 1.5 |
| 12 | real | image-left | Real environments reflect, bend, scatter and absorb signals | Reflection, diffraction, scattering, absorption; path loss ∝ dⁿ with n = 2 free space, 2.7–3.5 urban cellular, 4–6 obstructed indoors (section 8). Image placeholder: a city street with buildings | evidence | 2 |
| 13 | multipath | bullets | Multipath makes the signal fade over half a wavelength | Multipath copies add or cancel; about 6 cm at 2.4 GHz; delay spread; Doppler f_d = v/λ, 30 m/s car at 2 GHz gives up to 200 Hz (section 9) | story | 2 |
| 14 | budget-formula | formula | A link budget adds every gain and loss in decibels | P_r (dBm) = P_t + G_t + G_r − L; example 20 + 2 + 2 − 80 = −56 dBm (section 10) | evidence | 1.5 |
| 15 | budget-flow | diagram | Wi-Fi at 100 m arrives at −56 dBm, 34 dB above sensitivity | +20 dBm, +2 dBi, −80 dB, +2 dBi, −56 dBm; sensitivity −90 dBm (example value); margin 34 dB; margin absorbs walls, fading and bad days (section 10) | story | 2 |
| 16 | part2 | section | Part 2: how fast can we send data? | Modulation, bandwidth and noise set the data rate (sections 11 and 12) | signpost | 0.5 |
| 17 | modulation | bullets | Modulation changes amplitude, frequency or phase to carry bits | AM/ASK, FM/FSK, PSK, QAM; bits per symbol = log₂(points) (section 11) | evidence | 1.5 |
| 18 | constellation | chart | Each extra bit doubles the points and needs a cleaner signal | Column chart of bits per symbol: BPSK 1, QPSK 2, 16-QAM 4, 64-QAM 6, 256-QAM 8, 1024-QAM 10, 4096-QAM 12 (section 11); adaptive modulation: 256-QAM near the router | evidence | 1.5 |
| 19 | shannon | formula | Shannon: bandwidth and SNR set the maximum data rate | C = B·log₂(1 + SNR), SNR as a linear ratio; 20 MHz, SNR 30 dB (ratio 1000) gives about 199 Mbit/s per spatial stream (section 12) | evidence | 2 |
| 20 | levers | bullets | Bandwidth is the strongest lever; SNR helps only logarithmically | Rate grows linearly with bandwidth and logarithmically with SNR; OFDM subcarriers used by 802.11a/g, LTE, 5G NR; MIMO adds streams (section 12) | story | 1 |
| 21 | access | rows | Four multiple-access schemes separate users | FDMA (1G AMPS), TDMA (2G GSM, 8 slots per 200 kHz carrier), CDMA (3G UMTS, IS-95), OFDMA (4G LTE, 5G NR, Wi-Fi 6) (section 13) | evidence | 1.5 |
| 22 | duplex | bullets | Two-way links use FDD (separate frequencies) or TDD (taking turns) | FDD vs TDD; TDD shifts uplink/downlink capacity easily; Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CA, listen before talking and back off (section 13) | evidence | 1.5 |
| 23 | cells | diagram | Small cells reuse frequencies, so capacity multiplies | Cell grid with frequency reuse (letters illustrative); handover as a user moves; smaller cells mean more reuse (section 14). Image placeholder: a small-cell site on a city street | evidence | 2 |
| 24 | regulation | two-column | Regulators split spectrum into licensed and unlicensed bands | Licensed: operator buys exclusive rights, cellular. Unlicensed: anyone within power rules, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. ITU coordinates; FCC (US), Ofcom (UK); 2.4 GHz ISM band 2.400–2.4835 GHz; 1,200 MHz of 6 GHz opened in 2020 (section 15) | evidence | 1.5 |
| 25 | systems | rows | Same physics, different trade-offs across five systems | Bluetooth 2.4 GHz about 10 m; Wi-Fi 2.4, 5, 6 GHz tens of metres indoors; 4G LTE; 5G mid-band about 3.5 GHz; 5G mmWave 24–40 GHz about 100–300 m line of sight (section 16) | evidence | 1.5 |
| 26 | quiz-1 | bullets | Quiz (1 of 2): check your understanding | Questions 1 to 3 from section 18; answers in notes and on slide 28 | question | 1.5 |
| 27 | quiz-2 | bullets | Quiz (2 of 2): check your understanding | Questions 4 to 6 from section 18 | question | 1.5 |
| 28 | answers | bullets | Answers | Answers from section 18, revealed one per click | evidence | 1 |
| 29 | summary | two-column | Summary: nine ideas to take away | Section 17 summary items, grouped as how far, how fast, how many; the last line is what students now have | contribution | 1.5 |

**Total**: 29 slides, about 45.5 minutes (91% of the slot; the rest is for questions).
**Restatements of the story**: slides 2 (agenda), 16 (part 2 signpost), 29 (summary), each said a different way.

Wireless 101 · Module 1

How wireless communication works

By the end you will be able to say how far a signal goes, how fast it can carry data, and how many users can share the air.

[Presenter name]Wireless 101[Date]

Welcome. This is the first module, and it has one job: give you the vocabulary and the arithmetic that every later module uses. Read the subtitle aloud. It is the promise for the next 45 minutes. Students with no radio background should not worry: we start from the physics they already know and build up.

Every wireless system answers three questions

  1. How far can the signal go? propagation, path loss, link budget
  2. How fast can we send data? modulation, bandwidth, noise
  3. How many users can share the air? multiple access, cells, regulation

This is the thesis of the whole module, and you will hear it three times. Everyday examples to name while you talk: Wi-Fi, cellular (4G and 5G), Bluetooth, GPS, broadcast radio and TV, RFID tags and satellite links. Each one answers the same three questions. The three parts of today's lecture follow these questions, in this order.

From Maxwell's equations to 5G took more than a century

  1. 1865

    Maxwell

    Equations predict electromagnetic waves

  2. 1886–88

    Hertz

    Generates and detects radio waves in the lab

  3. 1901

    Marconi

    Receives a transatlantic radio signal

  4. 1979–83

    1G

    First analog cellular networks

  5. 1997

    Wi-Fi

    First IEEE 802.11 standard

  6. 2019

    5G

    First commercial 5G networks

Walk the timeline left to right. The key point is in the takeaway: each generation mainly changed how efficiently the same spectrum is used, not the physics. Other dates in the module's table: GSM 2G first call in Finland in 1991, Bluetooth 1.0 in 1999, and first commercial 4G LTE in Stockholm and Oslo in 2009. Note that Maxwell's 1865 equations to 2019 is about 150 years; the module's own takeaway says about 120, so quote the dates, not that number.

Wavelength is the speed of light divided by frequency

λ = c / f
λ
wavelength, in metres
c
speed of light, ≈ 3 × 108 m/s
f
frequency, in hertz (Hz)

100 MHz → 3 m · 2.4 GHz → 12.5 cm · 28 GHz → about 1.07 cm

A radio wave travels at the speed of light, so its frequency and wavelength are linked by one formula. Work the first example aloud: 3 × 10⁸ divided by 100 × 10⁶ gives 3 metres, the size of FM radio. Then 2.4 GHz gives 12.5 cm, which is Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. The number to remember: higher frequency means shorter wavelength.

A radio wave is an oscillating electric and magnetic field

Click one: the wave draws itself from left to right. Click two: the distance between two peaks is one wavelength, lambda. Click three: the speed is the speed of light, and frequency counts oscillations per second. This is the only picture of a radio wave you need for the module. Ask: if frequency doubles, what happens to the peaks? They get closer together.

The radio spectrum runs from 3 kHz to 300 GHz

Click one: the bands appear. The spectrum is split into eight named bands by the ITU. Click two: the arrow draws. Click three: the trade-off. Low frequencies travel far and go through buildings, but carry little data. High frequencies carry lots of data but do not travel far. Ask the room which band their phone uses: the cellular band is UHF.

Decibels turn multiplying gains into adding them

dB = 10 · log₁₀ (P₂ / P₁)
dB
ratio between two powers
dBm
power relative to 1 mW: 10 · log₁₀(P / 1 mW)
dBi
antenna gain relative to an ideal isotropic antenna

Signal powers in a real link range over many orders of magnitude, so we use a logarithmic scale. Three units: dB compares two powers, dBm is an absolute power relative to 1 milliwatt, and dBi is antenna gain relative to an ideal isotropic antenna. Keep the principle: in dB, gains and losses add and subtract. That is why link budgets are easy.

Three rules of thumb cover most link arithmetic

+3 dB≈ double the power (−3 dB ≈ half)
+10 dB= ten times the power (−10 dB = one tenth)
0 dBm= 1 mW (30 dBm = 1 W, −30 dBm = 1 µW)

Put these three on the board and keep them there. Let students do the arithmetic: 20 dBm is 100 mW, because 20 is 10 plus 10, which is ten times ten times the 1 mW reference. Sanity check: 1 W is 30 dBm, which is 0 dBm plus 30, so one thousand times 1 mW.

Antenna gain focuses power; it does not create it

  • An antenna converts current into a radio wave, and back again.
  • Isotropic antenna: the 0 dBi reference. Half-wave dipole: 2.15 dBi.
  • Fence: gain does not add energy. A directional antenna sends the same power into a narrower beam.
  • Phones and home routers use omnidirectional antennas; point-to-point links use directional ones.

This is the idea students get wrong most often. A high-gain antenna is not an amplifier: it concentrates the same power into a narrower beam, like a torch with a focused lens. Ask: why does a home router not use a dish? Because the signal has to go in all directions to reach phones around the room. Modern systems steer beams electronically with arrays, MIMO and beamforming, which we meet in Module 2.

Free-space path loss grows with distance and frequency

FSPL (dB) = 20 · log₁₀(d) + 20 · log₁₀(f) + 32.44
d
distance, in km
f
frequency, in MHz

Doubling the distance adds about 6 dB · doubling the frequency adds about 6 dB

Even in empty space the power spreads over a growing sphere, so received power falls with distance. Note the units: kilometres and megahertz. The two rules of thumb are the most useful part. Doubling distance costs 6 dB, and doubling frequency also costs 6 dB. Ask the room to predict the loss at 200 m before the next slide, then check.

Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz over 100 m loses about 80 dB

80dB

Free-space path loss, worked: 20·log₁₀(0.1) = −20.0; 20·log₁₀(2400) = 67.6; −20.0 + 67.6 + 32.44 ≈ 80 dB.

Module 1, section 7 (worked example)

Walk the three terms on the board, then reveal the number. Note that 2.4 GHz is 2400 MHz in the formula, and 100 m is 0.1 km. The lesson: an 80 dB loss is a very large number, and the link still works, because the transmitter, antenna gains and receiver sensitivity are all designed around it. That is the next part of the module.

Real environments reflect, bend, scatter and absorb signals

  • Reflected by large flat surfaces: buildings, the ground, walls.
  • Diffracted around edges, reaching shadowed areas.
  • Scattered by objects smaller than a wavelength: foliage, street signs.
  • Absorbed by concrete, water and human bodies.
  • Path loss grows as dⁿ: n = 2 in free space, 2.7–3.5 urban cellular, 4–6 obstructed indoors.

Free space is the ideal. Real signals do four things, and the exponent n captures how strongly the environment changes the loss with distance. Read the exponent table in the notes: free space 2; in a building with line of sight 1.6 to 1.8; urban cellular 2.7 to 3.5; shadowed urban cellular 3 to 5; obstructed in a building 4 to 6. The bigger n is, the faster the signal dies.

Multipath makes the signal fade over half a wavelength

  • Reflections give the receiver several delayed copies of the signal.
  • Copies in phase add up; copies out of phase cancel.
  • At 2.4 GHz, half a wavelength is about 6 cm: move that far and the signal can drop sharply.
  • Delay spread: echoes that arrive spread out in time overlap symbols.
  • Doppler: fd = v / λ. A car at 30 m/s receiving 2 GHz sees up to 200 Hz shift.

Multipath is the main enemy of a wireless link. Demonstrate it: stand two students apart and have them clap in time, then out of time. In phase they are louder; out of phase they cancel. Fast fading is that effect at small scale. Slow fading, from buildings and hills over tens of metres, is the other kind. Defences: diversity with several antennas, MIMO, error-correcting codes and OFDM, which we reach in Part 2. Doppler: 30 divided by 0.15 gives 200 Hz.

A link budget adds every gain and loss in decibels

Pr (dBm) = Pt + Gt + Gr − L
Pt
transmit power, dBm
Gt, Gr
antenna gains, dBi
L
losses, dB (path loss and others)
Pr
received power, dBm

Wi-Fi, 100 m: 20 + 2 + 2 − 80 = −56 dBm

This is the formula engineers use every day. Every term is in decibels, so it is simple addition. Gains add and losses subtract. Put the Wi-Fi example on the board: 20 dBm from the transmitter, plus 2 and 2 from the antennas, minus 80 dB of path loss, gives minus 56 dBm at the receiver.

Wi-Fi at 100 m arrives at −56 dBm, 34 dB above sensitivity

Click one: the five blocks. Clicks two to five: the arrows draw from transmitter to receiver, and the total is −56 dBm. Click six: compare with the receiver's sensitivity, −90 dBm in this example. The difference is the link margin, 34 dB. A link with no margin drops out the moment the environment gets worse, so margin is what you design for.

Part 2

How fast can we send data?

Modulation, bandwidth and noise set the data rate.

We have covered how far a signal can go. Now the question is how many bits per second get through that link. The answer comes from how we put bits on the wave, and from a limit set by bandwidth and noise.

Modulation changes a wave's amplitude, frequency or phase

  • Amplitude: AM (analog), ASK (digital).
  • Frequency: FM (analog), FSK (digital).
  • Phase: PSK (digital).
  • Amplitude and phase together: QAM (digital).
  • Bits per symbol = log₂(number of points in the constellation).

A pure carrier wave carries nothing. We modulate it by changing one property. Ask: how many bits does a symbol carry if there are 4 points? log base 2 of 4 is 2. Give the room a moment before the next slide: 2 points gives 1 bit, 16 points gives 4 bits, 256 points gives 8 bits.

Each extra bit doubles the points and needs a cleaner signal

More points per symbol means more bits, but the points sit closer together.

Read the bars left to right. Each extra bit doubles the number of points in the constellation, and that is why the bars get taller. The catch is the dark side: denser constellations need a higher SNR, because the points are closer together. That is why modern radios adapt. Near the router you get 256-QAM; at the edge of coverage you drop to BPSK or QPSK. Mention Wi-Fi 6 uses 1024-QAM and Wi-Fi 7 uses 4096-QAM.

Shannon: bandwidth and SNR set the maximum data rate

C = B · log₂(1 + SNR)
C
maximum error-free rate, bit/s
B
bandwidth, in Hz
SNR
as a linear ratio, not in dB

20 MHz, SNR 30 dB (ratio 1000): 20 × 10⁶ · log₂(1001) ≈ 199 Mbit/s per spatial stream

This is Shannon–Hartley, the most important formula in the module. C is the theoretical ceiling for error-free data. Be careful with SNR: the formula needs the linear ratio. 30 dB is a ratio of 1000. Work the example aloud: log base 2 of 1001 is about 9.97, times 20 million gives about 199 Mbit/s per spatial stream. That is a ceiling, not a typical speed.

Bandwidth is the strongest lever; SNR helps only logarithmically

  • More bandwidth: the rate grows linearly with it.
  • More SNR: the rate grows only logarithmically.
  • New standards add wider channels and new bands, and MIMO adds parallel streams.
  • OFDM splits a wide channel into many narrow subcarriers, robust to multipath. Used by Wi-Fi (802.11a/g onward), 4G LTE and 5G NR.

Ask the room: which is better, doubling bandwidth or doubling SNR? Shannon says bandwidth, because doubling bandwidth doubles the rate, while doubling SNR adds only a little. This explains why every new standard grabs more spectrum. OFDM is the technique that makes wide channels survive multipath, and it is a bridge to the multiple-access part.

Four multiple-access schemes separate users

  1. By frequency

    1G AMPS

  2. By time slot

    2G GSM, 8 slots per 200 kHz carrier

  3. By code

    3G UMTS (WCDMA), IS-95

  4. By groups of subcarriers and time

    4G LTE, 5G NR, Wi-Fi 6

Multiple access answers how many users share one channel. Each row is one way to separate them: frequency, time, code, or subcarriers. The highlighted row is the one you will meet most: 4G, 5G and Wi-Fi 6 all use OFDMA. Ask: why is the 1G row a frequency split? Because each call got its own frequency channel.

Two-way links use FDD (separate frequencies) or TDD (taking turns)

  • FDD: separate frequencies for uplink and downlink, at the same time.
  • TDD: the same frequency, taking turns in time.
  • TDD makes it easy to shift capacity between uplink and downlink.
  • Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CA: devices listen before talking and back off if the channel is busy.

Duplexing is how one device both sends and receives. FDD uses two frequencies, one for each direction, so both happen at once. TDD uses one frequency and switches turns, which is easy to rebalance. Wi-Fi does not schedule users at all; it uses listen-before-talk, so it is a different kind of sharing.

Small cells reuse frequencies, so capacity multiplies

Click one: the grid of cells. Click two: a handover path draws between two cells. Click three: the text. The idea is that a single powerful tower covers a city poorly, while many small, low-power cells let the same frequencies be reused. More reuse means more capacity. That is why dense cities use small cells and 5G millimetre-wave sites. The letters are only a picture of reuse; real plans depend on the network.

A small cell is a low-power base station

  • Low power keeps each cell's coverage local.
  • Handover moves a call or session to the next cell without dropping it.

Backup image slide for the cell idea. Show the photo and point out that the station is small and low-power. If time is short, skip this slide; it is marked as skippable in play.

Regulators split spectrum into licensed and unlicensed bands

Licensed

An operator buys exclusive rights, often at auction. Predictable and interference-managed.

Example: cellular networks

Unlicensed

Anyone may transmit within power rules. Free, but shared and congested.

Example: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, many IoT devices

Spectrum is a limited public resource, so it is regulated. The ITU coordinates globally, and national regulators allocate locally, for example the FCC in the United States and Ofcom in the United Kingdom. The 2.4 GHz ISM band runs from 2.400 to 2.4835 GHz and is shared by Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and microwave ovens. In 2020 the FCC opened 1,200 MHz of the 6 GHz band, from 5.925 to 7.125 GHz, for unlicensed use, which Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 use.

Same physics, different trade-offs across five systems

  1. 2.4 GHz · about 10 m (typical) · unlicensed

  2. 2.4, 5, 6 GHz · tens of metres indoors · unlicensed

  3. 600 MHz – 2.6 GHz (varies by country) · hundreds of metres to km · licensed

  4. about 3.5 GHz · hundreds of metres · licensed

  5. 24–40 GHz · about 100–300 m, line of sight · licensed

Each row is the same physics from this module. Frequency sets range and penetration. Bandwidth and SNR set speed. The access scheme and licensing set how many can share. Ask: why does mmWave reach only 100 to 300 m? Because its frequency is high, and high frequencies lose more and are blocked more easily.

Quiz

Check your understanding (1 of 2)

  1. What is the wavelength of a 5 GHz signal?
  2. Convert 100 mW to dBm.
  3. A link has 70 dB of path loss at 50 m. Roughly how much is it at 100 m in free space?

Give the room two minutes to work these on paper, then move on. Answers are on the answers slide, and in the notes here: question 1 is 6 cm; question 2 is 20 dBm; question 3 is about 76 dB, because doubling distance adds about 6 dB.

Quiz

Check your understanding (2 of 2)

  1. Which carries more bits per symbol, QPSK or 64-QAM, and what does it cost?
  2. Using Shannon, which raises capacity more at high SNR: doubling bandwidth or doubling SNR?
  3. Name the multiple-access technique used by 4G and 5G.

Take a show of hands on question 5 before you reveal it. Answers: question 4 is 64-QAM, 6 bits against 2, and it needs a higher SNR. Question 5 is doubling bandwidth. Question 6 is OFDMA.

Answers

  1. 6 cm (λ = c / f = 3 × 10⁸ / 5 × 10⁹)
  2. 20 dBm (10 · log₁₀(100 mW / 1 mW))
  3. About 76 dB (doubling the distance adds about 6 dB)
  4. 64-QAM: 6 bits against 2 for QPSK; it needs a higher SNR
  5. Doubling bandwidth (rate grows linearly with B)
  6. OFDMA

Reveal one answer per click, and let students check their own work. For question 3, the free-space figure is an estimate that uses the 6 dB rule; the original measurement at 50 m was in a real environment, so this is the free-space approximation the module asks for.

Summary: nine ideas to take away

How far

  1. λ = c / f: higher frequency, smaller antennas, more bandwidth, shorter range.
  2. Decibels add: 0 dBm = 1 mW; +3 dB ≈ ×2; +10 dB = ×10.
  3. FSPL ≈ 80 dB at 100 m and 2.4 GHz; each doubling adds 6 dB.
  4. Link budget: Pr = Pt + Gt + Gr − L; keep a margin.

How fast

  1. Modulation packs bits per symbol; denser needs more SNR.
  2. Shannon: C = B · log₂(1 + SNR); bandwidth is the strongest lever.

How many

  1. FDMA → TDMA → CDMA → OFDMA; FDD vs TDD; cells reuse frequencies.
  2. Regulators split spectrum into licensed and unlicensed bands.

Close on the three questions. How far: a link budget decides it, and margin protects it. How fast: bandwidth is the strongest lever. How many: multiple access and cells share the air. You now have the vocabulary and the arithmetic. Next module we go deeper into antennas and propagation: radiation patterns, MIMO and beamforming. Thank you for your attention, and well done on the quiz.
